q: You are motoring out of Dartmouth on a calm morning with the log speed steady. How far through the water have you run by now?
You time the boat between two log readings to check her speed under the new sail plan. What is your speed through the water?
why: 2.6 M in 20 min, a third of an hour: 2.6 × 3 = 7.8 kn. 20 min is 0.33 h, not 0.20 h.

q: You are running along the north coast of Brittany at a steady speed over the ground. When do you reach the fairway buoy?
ref: Chartwork — speed made good and ETA

q: You check the log against the plotter at slack water before a long passage. What does the difference tell you?
a: The log under-reads: clear the paddlewheel
o: A fair stream of 1.5 kn is running
The plotter over-reads: trust the log
Leeway is adding 1.5 kn over the ground
why: At slack water SOG should equal log speed; a log 1.5 kn low with weed about is a fouled paddlewheel.
ref: Navigation — the log and its error

q: Your log over-read on the measured run. Since the 0800 fix it shows this reading. What distance through the water do you lay off?
why: The log reads 2.2 for 2.0: divide by 1.1. 16.5 ÷ 1.1 = 15.0 M (not 16.5 less 10%).
ref: Navigation — the log and its error

fig.title: Log calibration
lines: Measured run: true 2.0 M, log 2.2 M

q: You leave the fix steering a steady course, with no stream and no leeway. Where do you mark the 1412 DR?
why: 1300 to 1412 is 1 h 12 min = 1.2 h; 5.0 × 1.2 = 6.0 M along the course steered.

q: The plotter has failed. From the log entries, where is your 1000 DR from the 0800 fix?
why: 6.0 M on 090°T, then 8.0 M on 160°T, end to end: the DR is 11.5 M on 131°T. Distances don't add.

q: You have laid off the course to the next waypoint on the chart. The boat has no deviation on this heading. What course do you give the helmsman?
why: True to magnetic: add westerly variation — 247° + 3° = 250°M.

q: You give the helmsman the course for the next leg across Lyme Bay. Which compass course do you write on the board?
Your helmsman has steered a steady compass course all watch. Which true course do you lay off for the DR?
why: Read the card for the ship's head: 312°C − 4°W = 308°M; + 1°E = 309°T.

q: Off Start Point you alter course for the next leg. Which true course do you plot for the new leg?
why: Read the card again for the new heading: 200°C − 3°W = 197°M; + 1°E = 198°T.

q: In the Aegean, you work out the compass course for the night leg from Kos. What do you give the helmsman?
why: 058°T − 4°E = 054°M; + 2°W deviation = 056°C. East is least, west is best.

q: The plotter is set to show magnetic. You want to draw your ground track on the paper chart. Which line do you draw?
why: Magnetic to true: subtract westerly variation — 085°M − 3°W = 082°T.
ref: Navigation — the plotter: heading, COG, SOG

q: You are close-hauled on port tack with the wind as shown. Which water track do you plot?
why: Leeway pushes you away from the wind: wind on the port side, so 085° + 7° = 092°T.

q: You take a bearing of your wake with the hand-bearing compass to measure leeway. What do you plot?
why: Dead astern the wake would bear 030°; it bears 022°, so 8° leeway, to port on starboard tack: 202°M.

q: You plan three legs for tomorrow under sail. Which leeway do you allow for each?
why: Leeway is greatest close-hauled in a breeze, small on a reach and nil running before the wind.

q: A Meltemi leg in the Aegean, with no stream to apply. Where do you plot the 1200 position from the 1000 fix?
why: Wind on the port beam pushes you to starboard: 120° + 6° = 126°T; 6.0 kn × 2 h = 12.0 M.

q: You plan a cross-tide leg past a drying ledge. Which line do you check against the ledge?
a: The ground track, with the stream applied
o: The water track you will steer along
The heading line given to the helmsman
The DR line from the course and the log
why: The boat moves over the ground: only the ground track shows where the stream takes you.
ref: Chartwork — ground track and water track

q: You draw the one-hour triangle for an EP and mark each line with its arrowheads. Which line gets three?
a: B: the stream's set and rate
o: A: the heading and the log distance
C: the course and speed over ground
A: the course steered through the water
why: Convention: water track one arrowhead, ground track two, tidal stream three.

q: You cross with a stream that runs east for the first two hours and west for the last two, equally. What does your ground track look like?
a: A curve bowing east, back on the line at the end
o: A straight line along the rhumb line
A straight line east of the rhumb line
A curve ending east of the destination
why: Steering one course, you are set east, then set back west by the same amount; you meet the line again at the end.

q: You are crossing the Channel south of the Isle of Wight with no leeway. Where do you plot the 0800 EP?
why: Water track 6.0 M east, then the hour's stream 2.0 M south from its end: 108°T, 6.3 M.

q: You work up the EP from the log book after two hours on the wind. Where do you plot the 1200 EP?
why: Wind on the port side: water track 045°T, 11.0 M; add both hours' streams end to end: 049°T, 8.3 M.

q: The almanac shows this diamond near your track. Where is your EP at the end of the hour, from its start?
You work up an EP for the 40 minutes since the fix. What length of stream do you lay off?
You want to make good the track from A to B. Which course do you steer, and what SOG do you expect?
why: Aim up-tide: sin⁻¹(1.5 ÷ 5.0) = 17°, so 090° + 17° = 107°T; SOG along the track = 5.0 × cos 17° = 4.8 kn.

q: You must make good 180°T to the harbour entrance on a beam reach. What compass course do you give the helmsman?
why: Stream: steer 191.5°T; wind from W, so 5° up into it = 196.5°T; + 2°W = 198.5°M; − 2°E = 197°C.

q: You plan the crossing from A to B as a single two-hour triangle. Which course do you steer?
why: Two hours of stream add to 3.6 M on 146°T; a 12.0 M arc from its end meets the track: steer 028°T.

q: In a cross-stream you keep turning to point the bow straight at the waypoint on the plotter. What happens to your track?
a: It curves down-tide and you sail further
o: It stays on the rhumb line as you correct
It curves up-tide and you arrive early
It is the same as steering one CTS
why: Chasing the bearing turns you up-tide late: you are set down-tide on a curve and cover more ground. Steer the worked CTS.

q: Your 1400 EP lies 2 M east of the planned track. From where do you work the new course to steer?
a: From the EP, to the next waypoint
o: From the DR, which leaves out the stream
From the departure point, as planned
From the planned track, abeam the EP
why: Always start a new triangle from your best position, here the EP, not from where you meant to be.

q: You plan this crossing. How do you steer it?
a: One course all the way: the streams cancel
o: A new course each hour against that hour's stream
The rhumb line, steering to keep XTE at zero
Down-tide first, to be up-tide at the end
why: Sum the hours' streams: they cancel, so one course on the track is the shortest way through the water.

q: You will cross the Channel on one course for the whole four hours. Which course do you steer?
why: Net stream over 4 h: 3.4 M east − 1.8 M west = 1.6 M east; aim off sin⁻¹(1.6 ÷ 22) ≈ 4° up-tide: 356°T.

q: What speed have you made good over the ground on this leg?
why: Speed made good uses the ground distance: 12.5 M in 2 h 30 min = 5.0 kn. The log's 14.0 M is through the water.
ref: Chartwork — speed made good and ETA

q: You head straight into the stream for the harbour. When do you arrive?
ref: Chartwork — speed made good and ETA

q: Your course-to-steer triangle is drawn. When do you expect to reach the next waypoint?
why: Use the SOG from the triangle: 7.0 ÷ 4.6 = 1.52 h = 1 h 31 min; 2215 + 1 h 31 = 2346.
ref: Chartwork — speed made good and ETA

fig.title: Night leg
lines: Next waypoint 7.0 M along the track

q: You have worked out a course to steer of 095°T for this cross-tide leg. What does the helmsman hold at 095°?
a: Heading: COG will differ by the stream
o: COG: it shows where the boat is going
Bearing to waypoint: keep it at 095°
why: A course to steer is a heading through the water; the COG is its result over the ground.
ref: Navigation — the plotter: heading, COG, SOG

q: From these steady readings, what set and rate is the stream giving you?
why: Stream = ground vector − water vector: 078°T 4.2 kn minus 095°T 5.6 kn leaves 2.0 kn setting 313°T.
ref: Navigation — the plotter: heading, COG, SOG

q: It is two hours before HW at the reference port. What stream do you use at this diamond for the hour?
why: Range 4.0 m is 2/3 of the way from neaps (2.0 m) to springs (5.0 m): 1.2 + 2/3 × 1.2 = 2.0 kn; set as given.

q: You are planning a leg in the Solent. Which atlas page gives the stream for it?
why: Each page covers half an hour either side of its time: 1400–1500 is centred on 1430, HW + 3 h.

fig.title: Tidal stream atlas
lines: One page per hour, HW−6 to HW+6

q: The atlas page shows this arrow off the headland. What rate do you apply there this hour?
why: 16,30 means neaps 1.6, springs 3.0 kn. 3.5 m is halfway from 2.2 to 4.8 m: 1.6 + 0.7 = 2.3 kn.

fig.title: Atlas page HW+1
lines: Mean ranges: springs 4.8 m, neaps 2.2 m

q: Your two-hour leg runs from 1000 to 1200. Which streams do you apply?
a: Half of HW+2, all of HW+3, half of HW+4
o: All of HW+2 and all of HW+3
All of HW+3 and all of HW+4
HW+2 only, taken for two hours
why: HW 0800: the HW+2 page covers 0930–1030, HW+3 1030–1130, HW+4 1130–1230. Take each for the time it applies.

fig.title: Tidal stream atlas
lines: Pages centred on each whole hour

q: Looking at tomorrow's legs, on which one is a plain DR, without an EP, good enough?
a: A: no stream and no leeway to apply
o: B: the streams cancel over six hours
C: the race runs too fast to plot
D: the ebb is along the track
why: DR leaves out stream and leeway. Only where both are nil, as motoring in a calm with no stream, is it enough.
ref: Chartwork — accuracy of DR and EP

fig.title: Tomorrow's legs
lines: A  Ionian, motoring in a calm, 2 h
B  across the Channel, 2 kn stream, 6 h
C  past the Alderney Race at night, 3 h
D  up the Solent against the spring ebb

q: It is 0600 on a night passage. How far from the 0600 EP could you really be?
why: Errors grow with time: up to 0.3 + 0.3 = 0.6 M each hour, four hours since the fix = 2.4 M. The shoal is inside it.
ref: Chartwork — accuracy of DR and EP

fig.title: 0600, night passage
lines: Last fix 0200; EP worked hourly since
Log and leeway good to ±0.3 kn
Shoal 2 M to leeward of the EP track

q: At night you close this headland. Your EP comes from a fix four hours old. What do you do?
a: Open the distance off and get a fix before turning
o: Turn at the EP time: the plot allows for the stream
Close the headland to pick up its light sooner
Turn when the log shows the planned distance
why: An old EP is an area, not a point. Keep sea room until a fix (a light, the depth) shows where you are.
ref: Chartwork — accuracy of DR and EP

q: Your fix does not match your EP. What do you allow for on the next leg?
a: About 0.5 kn more stream setting NE
o: About 1.5 kn more stream setting NE
About 0.5 kn more stream setting SW
No change: one fix proves nothing
why: 1.5 M of unexplained set in 3 h is about 0.5 kn towards the NE: add it to the next EP and check it at the next fix.
ref: Chartwork — accuracy of DR and EP

fig.title: Noon check
lines: 1200 fix lies 1.5 M NE of the 1200 EP

q: On your night watch the plotter dies. Which entries in the log let you carry on the plot?
a: Time, log reading and heading steered
o: Time, SOG and COG from the plotter
why: DR is rebuilt from time, distance run by the log and the heading; plotter COG/SOG are gone with it.

fig.title: Night watch, 0300
lines: Paper chart on the chart table

q: Between the hourly entries you bear away to clear a fishing fleet. What do you write in the log?
a: The time, log reading and new heading, now
o: Nothing until the next hourly entry
The new heading only, at the next hour
The plotter position, at the next hour
why: Every change of course is a new DR leg: it needs the time and log at the moment of the change.

fig.title: 0240, night
lines: Bear away to clear a fishing fleet

q: On a night passage the plotter works well. How do you keep the paper plot?
a: Mark a position each hour, with time and log
o: Plot only at the change of watch
Leave it until dawn: the plotter logs the track
Plot only if the plotter shows a fault
why: An hourly position on paper means a failure at 0300 costs one hour of DR, not the whole night.
ref: Navigation — keeping the plot at night

q: At 0200 the plotter freezes on a night passage. Which DR do you plot for 0200?
ref: Navigation — keeping the plot at night

q: You are motor-sailing along the coast to the next harbour. When do you arrive?
ref: Passage making — motor-sailing against the tide

q: You are motor-sailing into a foul stream. What does running at 2600 rpm buy you on this leg?
a: 48 min sooner for 4.4 l more fuel
o: 48 min sooner for 2.0 l more fuel
27 min sooner for 3.8 l more fuel
48 min sooner for the same fuel
why: SOG 4.0 vs 5.0 kn: 4 h 00 × 2.5 = 10.0 l against 3 h 12 × 4.5 = 14.4 l — 48 min sooner, 4.4 l more.
ref: Passage making — motor-sailing against the tide

q: You time the boat between two transits on the chart, motoring in flat water. What is your speed?
why: 4 cables = 0.4 M; 3 min is 1/20 of an hour: 0.4 × 20 = 8.0 kn. A cable is a tenth of a mile.

q: At night you close a rocky shore and plot a position every six minutes. How far do you lay off between plots?
why: Six minutes is a tenth of an hour: a tenth of 5.5 M is 0.55 M, 5.5 cables. Not 0.06 h.
ref: Navigation — keeping the plot at night

q: Fog closes in and you slow right down for the fairway buoy. When do you expect to reach it?
why: 9.5 ÷ 3.8 = 2.5 h = 2 h 30 min; 0610 + 2 h 30 = 0840. Half an hour, not 50 minutes.

fig.title: Fog, visibility 200 m
lines: Fairway buoy 9.5 M ahead on the DR

q: You run a measured distance both ways at the same revs to check the log in a steady stream. What is your real speed through the water at these revs?
why: Run speeds 8.0 and 5.0 kn: the stream adds to one and takes from the other, so their mean, 6.5 kn, is the speed through the water.
ref: Navigation — the log and its error

fig.title: Log check, 2200 rpm
lines: Run 1, with the stream: 2.0 M in 15 min
Run 2, against it: 2.0 M in 24 min
Log showed 7.0 kn on both runs

q: The paddlewheel jams at 1400 in a tidal stream and the log reads zero. How do you carry on the EP until it is cleared?
a: 5.5 kn from the rpm, then add the stream
o: 7.1 kn from the plotter, then add the stream
5.5 kn from the rpm, with no stream added
Stop the EP until the log is working
why: SOG already holds the stream: use it as the log speed and the stream counts twice. Take the speed through the water from the rpm.
ref: Navigation — the log and its error

q: The log has failed and fog makes you slow down. How far north of the 0700 fix is your 0830 DR?
The electrics fail at 0300. The log book has a gap: the 0130 alteration has no log reading. Where is your 0300 DR from the 0100 fix?
why: 12.0 M in 2 h is 6.0 kn: 3.0 M on 020°T to 0130, then 9.0 M on 110°T. End to end the DR is 9.5 M on 092°T.

fig.title: Log book, night
lines: Speed steady all night · no stream

q: After 30 M you find you applied the deviation for 045° to this whole leg. With no stream, where is the boat against the planned track?
why: 3°E used where 2°W applies: you headed 5° to port. 30 × sin 5° = 2.6 M, to the left of a SE track: NE.

q: You are close-hauled on port tack, steering this compass course. Which water track do you plot?
why: 040°C + 4°E = 044°M; − 2°W = 042°T. Port tack: leeway takes you to starboard, 042° + 6° = 048°T.

q: Handing over, your helmsman admits holding 3° to port of the course all leg. Roughly how far off the track are you?
why: 1 in 60 rule: 1° off puts you 1 M off in 60 M. 3° over 20 M: 20 × 3 ÷ 60 = 1.0 M, to port.
ref: Chartwork — accuracy of DR and EP

fig.title: End of the leg
lines: Steered 3° to port of the course

q: At the 0300 handover the helmsman tells you what he really steered. Which true heading do you lay off for the last hour's DR?
why: Plot what was steered, not what was ordered: 220°C + 2°E = 222°M; − 3°W = 219°T.
ref: Navigation — keeping the plot at night

q: On a charter catamaran you check the leeway by the wake. Which water track do you plot?
why: Wind on the starboard side pushes you to port: 300° − 11° = 289°T. A cat with stub keels slips far more than 6°.

q: Your catamaran's daggerboards are jammed up as you beat to windward. What leeway do you expect compared with boards down?
a: Much more: allow extra and check it by the wake
o: Less: the hulls grip better without boards
The same: leeway depends on the wind only
None: a catamaran makes no leeway
why: The boards are the cat's grip on the water: raised, she slides sideways far more. Measure it, don't guess.

q: At slack water, close-hauled on starboard tack, you read the plotter. What leeway is she making, and which water track do you plot?
why: With no stream, heading and COG differ by leeway alone: 250° − 243° = 7°, to port on starboard tack.
ref: Navigation — the plotter: heading, COG, SOG

q: Off the Brittany coast you work up the EP for 1130 from the 1000 fix. Where do you plot it?
why: Wind on the starboard beam: water track 310°T, 7.5 M in 1 h 30; then 1.5 h of stream, 2.1 M south: 295°T, 6.4 M.

q: You steer north for an hour and leave the stream out of the plot. Where are you really at the end of the hour?
why: A set is the direction the stream flows towards: 270°T carries you west, 1.8 M in the hour.

q: Today's tide is bigger than a mean spring. What rate do you use at this diamond for the hour?
why: 1.3 + (3.6 ÷ 3.0) × 1.2 = 2.7 kn: carry the interpolation on past springs rather than stopping at them.

fig.title: Diamond B, HW+1
lines: Mean ranges: springs 5.0 m · neaps 2.0 m

q: Your last fix was 1 h 30 min ago, and today's tide decides the rate at the diamond. How far has the stream carried you since?
why: Range 4.6 − 1.2 = 3.4 m: 1.4 + (1.4 ÷ 2.4) × 1.4 = 2.2 kn; for 1.5 h, 3.3 M. Use the range, not the HW height.

fig.title: Tidal data for today
lines: Tide table: HW 4.6 m, LW 1.2 m
Mean ranges: springs 4.4 m · neaps 2.0 m

q: The atlas and a diamond disagree for the same hour, at a spot right on your track. Which rate do you plot?
a: 1.8 kn, from the diamond on the spot
o: 1.2 kn, from the atlas for the area
1.5 kn, the mean of the two
1.2 kn, the atlas arrow nearest you
why: A diamond is the stream measured at that spot; the atlas draws the general pattern. On your track the diamond wins.

fig.title: HW−2, today's range
lines: Diamond F, on your track: 1.8 kn

q: Motoring with no leeway, you work up the EP two hours after the 0830 fix. Where do you plot it?
why: Halfway rates 1.5 then 2.0 kn: 10.0 M on 160°T, then 1.5 M on 060°T and 2.0 M on 075°T: 141°T, 10.5 M.

fig.title: Diamond C · HW 1030
lines: Today: halfway between springs and neaps

q: Your crew plotted the 1100 EP this way: an hour of the plotter's COG and SOG from the fix, then the hour's stream from its end. What do you tell them?
a: The stream is in twice: COG and SOG hold it
o: Correct: COG and SOG are through the water
Correct, but add the leeway on top
Wrong order: lay the stream off first
why: COG and SOG are over the ground, stream included. Plot them alone, or the heading and log plus the stream.
ref: Navigation — the plotter: heading, COG, SOG

q: On the paper chart you mark the 0300 position worked from the log, the heading and the tidal stream. Which symbol do you draw?
a: A triangle round the dot, with the time
o: A circle round the dot, with the time
A short line across the track, with the time
A square round the dot, with the time
why: By convention a fix is a circled dot, an EP a dot in a triangle, a DR a line across the track; always add the time.

q: You plan two legs at the same speed, with the same strength of stream on each. Which leg needs the bigger aim-off, and which loses more speed?
a: B more aim-off; A loses more speed
o: A more aim-off; B loses more speed
The same aim-off and speed on both
B more aim-off and more speed lost
why: A: aim 9° but SOG 3.6 kn; B: aim 17° but SOG 4.8 kn. A stream across costs angle; one on the bow costs speed.

q: You must make good 045°T to the next mark against this stream. Which course do you steer, and what SOG do you expect?
why: Its cross part sets you to starboard: aim 7° to port, 038°T. Most of it is on the bow: SOG only 4.3 kn.

q: Running south down the coast with the stream on your quarter, you want to make good 180°T. Which course do you steer, and what SOG?
why: The stream sets you east, so aim 16° west of the track: 196°T. Its along-track part is fair: SOG 6.2 kn.

q: The engine overheats and you throttle back to 3.0 kn on this cross-tide leg. Which course do you now steer, and what SOG?
why: Slower boat, same stream, bigger angle: sin⁻¹(1.5 ÷ 3.0) = 30°, 090° + 30° = 120°T; SOG 3.0 × cos 30° = 2.6 kn.

q: With the engine out and light airs, you try to draw the course to steer across this stream. What do you find?
a: The arc can't reach the track: no course works
o: Steer 053°T: the arc just meets it
why: Across the track the stream (3.0 kn) is faster than the boat (2.5 kn): the boat-speed arc never reaches the line.

q: You draw two hours of stream and the two-hour boat-speed arc. It cuts the track line 1.4 M beyond B. What does it tell you?
a: You reach B early: rework for the shorter time
o: Steer it: the extra miles are a margin
Steer it, and stop the clock at B
Add a third hour of stream to fit
why: You will reach B in under 2 h, so two hours of stream is too much. Rework with the time to B and its stream.

q: Three hours of hourly streams lie across this leg. Laying them all off in one triangle, which course do you steer?
why: The three hours add to 4.6 M on 090°T; a 16.5 M arc from its end meets the track: steer 325°T, 15° up-tide.

q: You must make good 270°T to B on a close reach, with the wind as given. Which course do you steer?
why: Stream: water track 256°T. The south wind on your port side pushes you north too, so steer 6° more into it: 250°T.

q: On a catamaran you must make good 090°T on a beam reach in this stream. Which course do you steer?
why: Stream: water track 080°T. The south wind pushes the cat 10° north, so steer 10° to starboard of it: 090°T.

q: Motoring this leg, you lay off both hours' streams in one triangle. Which compass course do you give the helmsman?
why: 2.6 M of stream on 296°T; a 12.0 M arc meets the track: 188°T. + 3°W = 191°M; − 2°E = 189°C.

q: You planned this crossing on one course, but you leave an hour late. Which course do you now steer?
why: 0900–1400 the streams net 3.0 M E − 5.0 M W = 2.0 M W; aim off sin⁻¹(2 ÷ 25) ≈ 5° east of south: 175°T.

fig.title: Channel crossing, one course
lines: 25.0 M due south at 5.0 kn: 5 h

q: Halfway across, the crew want to steer west to get back on the line. What do you tell them?
a: Hold 182°T: the west-going stream brings you back
o: Steer west of 182°T until the XTE is zero
Add the XTE to the course, in degrees
Follow the plotter's steer to the waypoint
why: One CTS is meant to drift off and come back. Steering for zero XTE fights the stream both ways and costs miles.

lines: One CTS 182°T for the 5 h crossing
Stream sets E until 1100, then W

q: Your single course to steer for this crossing gives a ground track bowing east, over a drying bank halfway. What do you do?
a: Work a CTS each hour to keep the track off the bank
o: Steer the one CTS: it ends on the line anyway
Steer the rhumb line and correct at the end
Steer the one CTS and watch the depth
why: One CTS is shortest only if the whole curve is safe. Where it crosses a hazard, plan each hour's course to keep clear.

q: Two hours after the last fix, your new fix lies on the track line but 1.0 M short of the EP. What do you suspect first?
a: Distance: the log or the stream's rate
o: Direction: leeway on the wrong side
why: An error along the track is one of distance: a log over-reading, or a foul stream stronger than plotted.

q: At the end of the leg your fix lies off the DR as shown. What heading error explains it?
a: 5° to starboard of the course set
o: 5° to port of the course set
8° to starboard of the course set
1.5° to starboard of the course set
why: 1 in 60: 1.5 M off in 18 M is 1.5 × 60 ÷ 18 = 5°. East of a northerly track means you headed to starboard.

fig.title: Motoring at slack water
lines: Fix lies 1.5 M east of the DR

q: You kept a plain DR from the 1000 fix. The 1200 fix lies as shown. What mean stream did you have?
why: DR to fix is the stream's work over 2 h: 2.4 M towards 200°T, so 1.2 kn setting 200°T.

q: Motoring along the coast, you compare the plotter with the log. What is the stream doing?
why: Heading and COG agree, so there is no cross set; SOG 6.8 against log 5.5 kn: a fair stream of 1.3 kn.
ref: Navigation — the plotter: heading, COG, SOG

lines: Steady for the last half hour

q: Motoring slowly in a swell, you watch the plotter's COG and SOG jump about. What do you use for the DR?
a: The compass heading and the log
o: The mean of the plotter's COG and SOG
The last steady COG and SOG you saw
The bearing and distance to the waypoint
why: At low speed in a seaway COG and SOG swing with every wave; the heading and the log give a steady DR.
ref: Navigation — the plotter: heading, COG, SOG

lines: Motoring slowly in a big swell

q: You join a cross-tide leg and the plotter shows this. What does its CTS figure give you?
a: A steer back to the line, with no stream in it
o: The heading that allows for the stream
The COG you will make good over the ground
why: With no tidal data the plotter's CTS is only the steer back to the route line. Work the stream yourself.

q: Your heading points well clear of the rocks, but the plotter's COG line runs onto them. Where is the boat going?
a: Along the COG line: alter up-tide now
o: Along the heading: the COG line lags
Between the two: they average out
Along the heading, once the stream eases
why: COG is the track over the ground, stream included; the heading only shows where the bow points.
ref: Navigation — the plotter: heading, COG, SOG

q: The plotter gives this ETA at the next harbour. When do you really expect to arrive?
why: To 1300 at 6.5 kn: 6.5 M. The last 6.5 M at 5.0 − 1.0 = 4.0 kn take 1 h 38: 1438. The plotter assumes today's SOG.
ref: Chartwork — speed made good and ETA

q: In thick fog the plotter screen goes blank. Where do you start the DR from?
a: The 0700 fix written in the log
o: The last plotter position you recall
The next waypoint on the route
The spot where the depth fits best
why: Restart from the last position you wrote down with its time and log: here 1.7 M on 270°M from the 0700 fix.

q: Your next fix is hours away. Which possible error moves your EP furthest from the truth?
why: Over 4 h: stream 1 kn × 4 = 4.0 M; heading 24 M × sin 5° = 2.1 M; leeway 1.3 M; log 3% of 24 M = 0.7 M.
ref: Chartwork — accuracy of DR and EP

q: In fog with no radar you close this coast to find the harbour, your EP good to about a mile. Where do you aim?

o: Straight at it, then search either side
0.5 M east of it, then follow the coast west
2 M west of it, then follow the coast west
why: Aim off by more than the EP error: when you meet the coast or the depth line, you know which way to turn.

q: You have beaten towards the windward mark for two hours. What speed have you made good towards it?
why: Each 6.0 M tack runs 45° off the bearing: 6.0 × cos 45° = 4.24 M towards the mark, twice: 8.5 M in 2 h = 4.2 kn.
ref: Chartwork — speed made good and ETA

q: Against a foul stream, how much time does hoisting the main save you on this leg?
why: SOG 4.0 vs 5.0 kn: 12.0 ÷ 4.0 = 3 h 00, 12.0 ÷ 5.0 = 2 h 24 — 36 min. Against the stream each knot counts for more.
